WHAT SCRIPTURE SAYS
What Scripture says of him
John the Baptist reproved "Herod the tetrarch" "for Herodias his brother Philip's wife, and for all the evils which Herod had done", and Herod "shut up John in prison". Luke 3:19–20

John had told him, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Matthew says Herod would have put him to death but "feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet". Mark 6:17–18 Matthew 14:3–5
Mark says Herodias wanted John dead, "but she could not: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy", and "heard him gladly". Mark 6:19–20

At his birthday supper the daughter of Herodias danced; he swore to give her whatever she asked, "unto the half of my kingdom". Prompted by her mother she asked for "the head of John the Baptist". "The king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake" he sent and had John beheaded in the prison. Mark 6:21–28 Matthew 14:6–11

Hearing of Jesus' works, he said, "It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead." In Luke he is "perplexed": "John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things? And he desired to see him." Mark 6:14–16 Luke 9:7–9
Some Pharisees warned Jesus, "Herod will kill thee." Jesus answered, "Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow". Luke 13:31–32
Jesus warned his disciples to "beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, and of the leaven of Herod". Mark 8:15

At the trial Pilate sent Jesus to Herod, who "was exceeding glad" and "hoped to have seen some miracle done by him". He questioned him "in many words; but he answered him nothing". Herod and his soldiers "set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe", and sent him back. Luke 23:7–11
"The same day Pilate and Herod were made friends together." Pilate told the accusers, "No, nor yet Herod" had found anything worthy of death in Jesus. Luke 23:12–15
The church in Jerusalem said in prayer that "both Herod, and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, were gathered together" against Jesus. Acts 4:27
Among those near him: Joanna, "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", who ministered to Jesus; and Manaen of the church at Antioch, "brought up with Herod the tetrarch". Luke 8:3 Acts 13:1

SCHÜRER (1890)
Tetrarch from Herod's death in 4 BC until Gaius (Caligula) deposed him, in the summer of AD 39 by Schürer's reckoning; his coins run to the forty-third year of his rule.
In Galilee, perhaps Tiberias
Keim and Volkmar, as reported by Schürer (1890)
They read Mark's guests, the "chief estates of Galilee", as placing the supper in Galilee. Schürer answers that the Gospels do not name the place. Mark 6:21 [14]
At Julias
Wieseler, as reported by Schürer (1890)
Wieseler moved the scene to Julias; Schürer sees no reason for it.[14]

WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture never uses the name Antipas; it calls him Herod.
The Gospels do not name the place where John was imprisoned and killed.
Scripture does not name the daughter of Herodias.
Scripture does not record how his rule ended.
Scripture does not say who the Herodians were (Matthew 22:16; Mark 3:6; 12:13), or how they were connected with him.
Scripture does not say why Pilate and Herod had been at enmity.
IDENTIFICATIONS THIS PAGE RELIES ON

From the textThe Gospels and Acts call him "Herod the tetrarch", and Luke "tetrarch of Galilee"; Luke names Philip as his brother. Scripture never uses the name Antipas. Matthew 14:1 Luke 3:1 Luke 3:19 Luke 9:7 Acts 13:1
Scholars' viewSchürer (1890) notes that Antipas is the only man called Herod who bore the title of tetrarch (his brother Philip was also a tetrarch, but is never called Herod).[12]

From the textThe Herod of Jesus' trial is the same man: Pilate sent Jesus to him on learning that he was a Galilean and "belonged unto Herod's jurisdiction". Acts 4:27 looks back on that day. Luke 23:6–7 Acts 4:27

From the textThree verses say only "Herod": Jesus' warning about "the leaven of Herod", Joanna "the wife of Chuza Herod's steward", and the Pharisees' "Herod will kill thee". They are taken as the tetrarch from their setting: Jesus' work in Galilee and on the road, after "Herod was dead" (Matthew 2:19) and before the "Herod the king" of Acts 12. Mark 8:15 Luke 8:3 Luke 13:31 Matthew 2:19 Acts 12:1
